prompt: Kangaroo Joey wants to jump through the maze. Joey starts in the square on the bottom left (see picture). The number of arrows decides how long the jump must be. A square with three arrows means that Joey has to jump over two squares in the direction of the arrows and land in the third square. Where will Joey leave the maze?

choices.text: Joey cannot leave the maze anywhere.

solutions.title: Follow the jumps one by one
solutions.body:
Number the rows 1 (top) to 5 (bottom) and the columns 1 (left) to 5 (right). Joey starts in row 5, column 1.

- Three arrows right: jump 3 squares right to row 5, column 4.
- Two arrows up: jump 2 up to row 3, column 4.
- One arrow left: to row 3, column 3.
- One arrow up: to row 2, column 3.
- Two arrows right: to row 2, column 5.
- One arrow up: to row 1, column 5.
- One arrow right: Joey jumps out of the maze through exit **B**.

**Answer: (B) B**

solutions.title: Check the exits backwards
solutions.body:
Ask which squares could send Joey out of each exit.

- Exit B is next to the top-right square, which has an arrow pointing right, out through B.
- That square is reached from the square below it (row 2, column 5, arrow up), which is reached by the double-right arrow in row 2, column 3.
- Following the arrows from the start (3 right, 2 up, 1 left, 1 up) lands exactly on that double-right square.

So the path from the start ends at B, and Joey never gets stuck in a loop.

**Answer: (B) B**

prompt: The picture shows the footprints of the first few jumps of a type of hopscotch. The prints show whether one is allowed to land in that square with the left foot, the right foot or both feet. Mia starts with both feet in the field with the number 1 and repeats the jumping pattern in the direction of the arrow. In which of the following squares is Mia allowed to land with her right foot only?

solutions.title: Find the repeating pattern
solutions.body:
The pattern of squares 1 to 4 is: both feet, left foot, both feet, right foot. Then it repeats.

- Right foot only: squares 4, 8, 12, 16, **20**, 24, ...
- These are exactly the multiples of 4.
- Of the choices, only 20 is a multiple of 4 ($20 = 5 \times 4$).

**Answer: (C) square no. 20**

solutions.title: Check each choice
solutions.body:
The pattern repeats every 4 squares, so look at the remainder after dividing by 4:

- remainder 1 or 3: both feet
- remainder 2: left foot
- remainder 0: right foot

Check: 10 → remainder 2 (left), 1 → both, 20 → remainder 0 (**right**), 22 → remainder 2 (left), 23 → remainder 3 (both).

**Answer: (C) square no. 20**

prompt: Dina has placed three building blocks behind a wall. From the front, the arrangement looks as shown in the picture on the right. What does the arrangement look like from behind?

solutions.title: Walk around to the other side
solutions.body:
When you walk behind the wall, left and right swap, and the wall is now at the back.

- From the front, the blocks are partly hidden by the wall. From behind, nothing hides them: they are fully visible, and the wall is behind them.
- The block that was on the right is now on the left, and the one on the left is now on the right.
- The block that is nearest to you from behind is the one that was farthest from you at the front, so it covers the blocks further back.

Only picture (B) shows the mirrored arrangement with the blocks fully visible in front of the wall.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Rule out wrong pictures
solutions.body:
- Any picture where the wall hides part of the blocks is wrong: from behind, the blocks stand in front of the wall.
- Any picture where the blocks are in the same left-to-right order as from the front is wrong: going around swaps left and right.
- Among the remaining pictures, check which block is in front: the wide medium block must cover part of the tall dark block, with the thin block at the left.

That leaves (B).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Mona wants to draw the figure shown without lifting her pen. The lengths of the segments are known. Mona can start her drawing anywhere and go over segments more than once. What is the minimum distance in cm that Mona has to move her pen across the paper?

solutions.title: Go back over the shortest segment
solutions.body:
The three segments (3 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm) meet at one point.

- Mona can draw two of them in one stroke, e.g. start at the end of the 3 cm segment and go to the end of the 2 cm segment.
- The third segment is a dead end: she has to go along it and come back, so she draws one segment twice.
- Best: draw the 1 cm segment twice. Start at the end of the 3 cm segment, go to the middle, down the 1 cm segment and back up, then along the 2 cm segment.

Distance: $3 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 7 cm**

solutions.title: Why 6 cm is impossible
solutions.body:
The figure has 3 free ends. A path without lifting the pen has only 2 ends (start and finish). So one free end is neither start nor finish: Mona must go to it and come back, drawing that segment twice.

- Doubling the 1 cm segment: $6 + 1 = 7$ cm.
- Doubling the 2 cm or 3 cm segment would give 8 or 9 cm.

The minimum is 7 cm.

**Answer: (B) 7 cm**

prompt: Pieter has a parcel that weighs 445 g and the eight weights shown. He places the parcel on the right scale pan (see picture). Pieter is allowed to place weights on either side of the scale. What is the minimum number of weights that he needs to balance the scale?

solutions.title: Find a way with 3 weights
solutions.body:
Put the 500 g weight on the left pan. The right pan then needs $500 - 445 = 55$ g more.

- Put 50 g and 5 g next to the parcel on the right: $445 + 50 + 5 = 500$.
- Both sides weigh 500 g: balanced with **3** weights.

Now check that fewer is impossible (see the other approach).

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Why 1 or 2 weights are not enough
solutions.body:
445 ends in 5. All weights except the 5 g weight end in 0, so the 5 g weight must be used, or the two sides can never be equal.

- 1 weight: it would have to be 445 g. There is none.
- 2 weights, one of them 5 g: the other weight would have to be $445 - 5 = 440$ g (both on the left) or $445 + 5 = 450$ g (5 g on the right). Neither exists.

So at least 3 weights are needed, and 3 works.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: Werner has a circular transparent piece of paper with some holes and lines. He folds it along the dashed line. What does the folded paper look like?

solutions.title: Fold one half onto the other
solutions.body:
Folding along the dashed line puts one half of the circle exactly on top of the other half, like a mirror.

- The lines and holes from both halves can be seen, because the paper is transparent.
- Reflect the lines from the right half onto the left half: together with the lines already there, they form two diamond shapes.
- The holes of both halves end up in 4 different places.

This is picture (C).

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Check details of each picture
solutions.body:
Because the paper is transparent, everything from both halves must be visible after folding.

- Holes: the left half has 2 holes and the right half has 2 holes in other places, so the folded paper shows **4** holes. (A), (B), (D) and (E) do not show 4 holes in the right places.
- Lines: the zigzag on the left and the mirrored zigzag from the right cross each other and make two diamonds.

Only (C) has both diamonds and 4 holes.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Two children are flying their kites. Which picture fits into the empty space so that each child is holding one kite?

solutions.title: Follow the strings
solutions.body:
Call the four string ends at the top of the empty square T1 to T4 (left to right) and the four at the bottom B1 to B4.

- Above the square: the girl's kite leads to T3, the boy's kite leads to T2, and T1 and T4 are joined to each other.
- Below the square: B1 leads to the girl, B4 leads to the boy, and B2 and B3 are joined to each other.

Piece (D) joins T1–B3, T2–B4, T3–T4 and B1–B2. Follow the girl: B1 → B2 → B3 → T1 → T4 → T3 → kite 1. Follow the boy: B4 → T2 → kite 2. Each child holds exactly one kite.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
Try each piece and trace a string from each child.

- In some pieces a child's string comes back down to the same side, so that child holds no kite.
- In (E), the two kites end up joined to each other, not to the children.
- In the others, one child ends up connected to both kites or to none.

Only (D) gives each child exactly one kite.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: There are six boxes on a lorry (see picture). A worker unloading the lorry is not allowed to pick up a box that has another one lying on top. He places every box either on the floor or on top of another box. Each box is only to be touched once. Which one of the following towers can the worker not build?

solutions.title: Write down the rules
solutions.body:
From the lorry picture:

- E and F lie on C, so E and F must be taken off before C.
- C lies on A and B, so C comes off before A and B.
- D lies on B, so D comes off before B.

A box in a tower is placed after the box under it. In tower (C), D sits on top of B, so B was taken off before D. But D lies on B on the lorry, so D must be taken off first. Impossible!

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Check that the other towers work
solutions.body:
Unloading order must respect: E, F before C; C before A and B; D before B.

- (A) E, F, C, D, A, B works.
- (B) E, F, D, C, A, B works.
- (D) F, E, C, D, B, A works.
- (E) E, F, D, C, B, A works.
- (C) needs B before D, which breaks the rule "D before B".

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Pia writes a number into each of the 16 little circles (see picture). Numbers in neighbouring circles differ by 1. She writes the number 5 into one of the circles and the number 13 into another one. How many different numbers does Pia write in the 16 circles?

solutions.title: Count the steps
solutions.body:
Each step to a neighbour changes the number by exactly 1. To go from 5 to 13 you need at least $13 - 5 = 8$ steps.

- There are 16 circles in a ring, so the two paths from the 5 to the 13 have lengths that add up to 16.
- Both paths need at least 8 steps, so both have exactly 8 steps.
- Then on both paths the numbers must go up by 1 every step: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.

The numbers used are 5 to 13: that is **9** different numbers.

**Answer: (A) 9**

solutions.title: Draw it
solutions.body:
Put 5 at the bottom of the ring. Going round the left side, you must reach 13 at the top in 8 steps, so you write 6, 7, ..., 12, then 13. Going round the right side, the same happens: 6, 7, ..., 12, 13.

Every number from 5 to 13 appears (each twice, except 5 and 13), and no other number appears.

$13 - 5 + 1 = 9$ numbers.

**Answer: (A) 9**

prompt: The picture on the right is 45 cm wide, 30 cm high and made up of identical rectangles. What is the area of one such rectangle?

solutions.title: Use the width, then the height
solutions.body:
Call the long side of a rectangle $L$ and the short side $w$.

- The bottom row has 5 lying rectangles: $5L = 45$, so $L = 9$ cm.
- Going up the picture: lying, standing, lying, standing, lying. That is 3 short sides and 2 long sides: $3w + 2L = 30$.
- $3w + 18 = 30$, so $3w = 12$ and $w = 4$ cm.

Area: $9 \times 4 = 36\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (E) 36 cm²**

solutions.title: Check with the choices
solutions.body:
From the bottom row, the long side is $45 \div 5 = 9$ cm, so the area must be a multiple of 9: only 27 and 36 are.

- Area 27 means short side 3: height $= 3 \times 3 + 2 \times 9 = 27$ cm. Too small.
- Area 36 means short side 4: height $= 3 \times 4 + 2 \times 9 = 30$ cm. Correct!

**Answer: (E) 36 cm²**

prompt: The rooms in a hotel are numbered in ascending order (No. 1, 2, 3, ...). No number is left out. Beaver Benji counts the digits of all the room numbers and finds the digit 2 fourteen times and the digit 5 three times. What is the biggest possible room number in this hotel?

solutions.title: Count the 5s, then the 2s
solutions.body:
- The digit 5 appears in 5, 15, 25, then in 35. Exactly three 5s means the last room is between 25 and 34.
- Count the 2s up to 29: 2, 12 (two of them), then 20 to 29 has ten 2s in the tens place plus one more in 22 (eleven). Total $1 + 1 + 11 = 13$.
- The 14th 2 is in 32. The next 2 would be in 42.

So the last room is between 32 and 34 (and at most 34 because of the 5s). The biggest possible is **34**.

**Answer: (C) 34**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
- 25 or 26: only 2, 12, 20–26 → $1 + 1 + 7 + 1 = 10$ twos (22 has two). Too few.
- 34: twos in 2, 12, 20–29 (11 twos), 32 → 14 twos; fives in 5, 15, 25 → 3 fives. Works!
- 35: a 4th five appears. No.
- 41: has 35 too, so 4 fives. No.

**Answer: (C) 34**

prompt: Christian cuts out four small grey squares from one big square. The white shape remains (see picture). This shape has half the area of the big square. The side lengths of the small grey squares are stated in the drawing. What is the perimeter of the white shape?

solutions.title: Find the big square first
solutions.body:
The grey squares have areas $1 + 4 + 9 + 36 = 50$.

- The white shape is half of the big square, so the grey part is the other half: the big square has area $2 \times 50 = 100$, and side length 10.
- Cutting a square out of a corner does not change the perimeter: the two edges you lose are replaced by two equal edges going in.

So the white shape has the same perimeter as the big square: $4 \times 10 = 40$.

**Answer: (B) 40**

solutions.title: Push the edges outwards
solutions.body:
Big square side: grey area $= 1 + 4 + 9 + 36 = 50$ is half, so the big square is $100$ and its side is 10.

Walk around the white shape. At each cut-out corner the path goes in and then out like a step. Push the horizontal step edges up/down and the vertical step edges left/right onto the big square's sides: they fill the sides exactly.

Perimeter $= 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 40$.

**Answer: (B) 40**

prompt: The number 2024 is made up of the four digits 2, 0, 2 and 4. How many different four-digit numbers bigger than 2024 can be formed with exactly those digits?

solutions.title: List them all
solutions.body:
A four-digit number cannot start with 0, so it starts with 2 or 4.

- Starting with 2 (the other digits are 0, 2, 4): 2024, 2042, 2204, 2240, 2402, 2420.
- Starting with 4 (other digits 0, 2, 2): 4022, 4202, 4220.

Bigger than 2024: 2042, 2204, 2240, 2402, 2420, 4022, 4202, 4220. That is **8** numbers.

**Answer: (E) 8**

solutions.title: Count all, then subtract
solutions.body:
- Starting with 4: the digits 0, 2, 2 can be arranged in 3 ways (the 0 goes in one of 3 places).
- Starting with 2: the digits 0, 2, 4 can be arranged in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways.

That is 9 numbers in total. The smallest of them is 2024 itself (it starts 20 and then 2 before 4). All others are bigger: $9 - 1 = 8$.

**Answer: (E) 8**

prompt: Simon has four cups with matching saucers (see picture). He places a randomly chosen cup on each saucer. Which statement is definitely true?

choices.text: It is certain that none of the 4 cups are on the matching saucer.
It is certain that exactly one cup is on the matching saucer.
It is impossible that exactly 2 cups are on the matching saucers.
It is impossible that exactly 3 cups are on the matching saucers.
It is impossible that all 4 cups are on the matching saucers.

solutions.title: Think about the last cup
solutions.body:
Suppose 3 cups are on their matching saucers.

- Then only one cup and one saucer are left over.
- That last cup must go on the last saucer, and it is its own matching saucer!
- So if 3 match, all 4 match. Exactly 3 matches can never happen.

**Answer: (D) It is impossible that exactly 3 cups are on the matching saucers.**

solutions.title: Find examples against the other statements
solutions.body:
- All 4 matching is possible (he might get lucky), so (A), (B) and (E) are false.
- Exactly 2 matching is possible: put cups 1 and 2 correctly and swap cups 3 and 4. So (C) is false.
- Exactly 3 matching is impossible, because the fourth cup would then have to be on its own saucer too.

**Answer: (D) It is impossible that exactly 3 cups are on the matching saucers.**

prompt: The picture on the right shows four rectangles that touch each other. What is the area of the rectangle with the question mark?

solutions.title: Find all the side lengths
solutions.body:
- Tall rectangle: area 45, width 5, so height $45 \div 5 = 9$ cm.
- Whole height 13, so the bottom rectangle is $13 - 9 = 4$ cm high. Its area is 40, so it is $40 \div 4 = 10$ cm wide.
- Right rectangle: width $16 - 10 = 6$ cm, area 48, so height $48 \div 6 = 8$ cm.
- ? rectangle: width $10 - 5 = 5$ cm, height $8 - 4 = 4$ cm.

Area: $5 \times 4 = 20\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (E) 20 cm²**

solutions.title: Use the whole L-shape
solutions.body:
From the side lengths found step by step: tall rectangle $5 \times 9$, bottom $10 \times 4$, right $6 \times 8$.

The tall rectangle, the ? rectangle and the bottom rectangle together, plus the right rectangle, fill the outline. The ? rectangle sits above the bottom one, right of the tall one and left of the right one: its width is $10 - 5 = 5$ and its top is at height 8 (the top of the right rectangle), its bottom at height 4.

$5 \times (8 - 4) = 20\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (E) 20 cm²**

prompt: Blind people use Braille, in which numbers and letters are displayed as a code with up to 6 tactile dots (black in the picture). The numbers 0 to 9 can be seen on the right. How many two-digit numbers have exactly four black dots?

solutions.title: Sort the digits by dots
solutions.body:
Count the black dots of each digit:

- 1 dot: 1
- 2 dots: 2, 3, 5, 9
- 3 dots: 0, 4, 6, 8
- 4 dots: 7

Four dots in total: $1 + 3$, $3 + 1$ or $2 + 2$ (a 4-dot digit would need a 0-dot partner, which doesn't exist).

- Tens 1, units 0/4/6/8: 4 numbers.
- Tens 4/6/8 (not 0!), units 1: 3 numbers.
- Both digits from 2, 3, 5, 9: $4 \times 4 = 16$ numbers.

Total: $4 + 3 + 16 = 23$.

**Answer: (E) 23**

solutions.title: List by tens digit
solutions.body:
Using the dot counts (1: one dot; 2, 3, 5, 9: two dots; 0, 4, 6, 8: three dots; 7: four dots):

- Tens digit 1 (1 dot): needs 3 more → 10, 14, 16, 18 (4).
- Tens digit 2, 3, 5 or 9 (2 dots): needs 2 more → 4 choices each, 16 numbers.
- Tens digit 4, 6 or 8 (3 dots): needs 1 more → 41, 61, 81 (3).
- Tens digit 7 (4 dots): would need 0 more dots, impossible.

$4 + 16 + 3 = 23$.

**Answer: (E) 23**

prompt: The two large squares have the same area. Parts of them are coloured grey (see picture). In the left square, the dots divide the sides into two equal pieces. In the right square, the dots divide the sides into three equal pieces. The four grey parts in the left square have a combined area of 9 cm². What is the area of the four grey parts in the right square?

solutions.title: Find the big square's area
solutions.body:
Left square: joining the midpoints of the sides makes an inner square. The four grey corner triangles fold exactly onto the inner square, so they are **half** of the big square.

- Big square: $2 \times 9 = 18\ \text{cm}^2$.

Right square: each grey square has a side that is one third of the big side, so it fits 9 times into the big square: area $18 \div 9 = 2\ \text{cm}^2$.

- Four grey squares: $4 \times 2 = 8\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (B) 8 cm²**

solutions.title: Use a 3-by-3 grid
solutions.body:
Divide the right square into a $3 \times 3$ grid using the dots. Each grey square is one of the 9 small squares, so the grey part is $\frac{4}{9}$ of the big square.

The left grey part is $\frac{1}{2}$ of the big square and equals 9 cm², so the big square is 18 cm².

$\frac{4}{9} \times 18 = 8\ \text{cm}^2$.

**Answer: (B) 8 cm²**

prompt: Annie wants to write the numbers 1 to 10 in the ten circles (see picture on the right). Each circle should have a different number. Annie wants the sum of the four numbers along each line to be exactly 23. Which number does she have to write in the circle with the question mark?

solutions.title: Add up all three lines
solutions.body:
There are three lines of 4 circles, and they all share the circle with the question mark.

- Adding the three line sums: $3 \times 23 = 69$.
- This counts every circle once, except the ? circle, which is counted 3 times (2 extra times).
- All numbers 1 to 10 add to $55$.

So $55 + 2 \times ? = 69$, which gives $2 \times ? = 14$ and $? = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

solutions.title: Look at the other nine circles
solutions.body:
If the ? circle holds $x$, then each line needs three more numbers adding to $23 - x$. The other 9 circles together add to $3 \times (23 - x)$.

They also add to $55 - x$. So $69 - 3x = 55 - x$, giving $2x = 14$, $x = 7$.

Check: the other lines need sums of 16, e.g. $1 + 5 + 10$, $2 + 6 + 8$, $3 + 4 + 9$. It works!

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt: The map shows the seven subway lines of a city. The stations are represented by circles. Martin wants to colour in the subway lines in the plan. If two lines have a common station, they must have different colours. What is the smallest number of different colours he can use?

solutions.title: Fewer than 3 is impossible, 3 works
solutions.body:
Lines 1, 2 and 4 all meet each other (line 2 crosses line 4 at a station and line 1 at a station, and line 1 crosses line 4). So these three need 3 different colours.

Now try 3 colours:

- The vertical lines 4, 5 and 6 never meet each other: give them all **red**.
- Lines 2 and 7 never share a station: give them **blue**.
- Lines 1 and 3 never share a station: give them **green**.

Check: every crossing is between a vertical line (red) and a horizontal/bent line (blue or green), or between 1 and 2, 1 and 7, or 3 and 7 (blue–green). All fine!

**Answer: (A) 3**

solutions.title: Group the lines that don't meet
solutions.body:
Look for lines that can share a colour because they have no common station:

- 4, 5, 6 are parallel vertical lines — no common station.
- Line 2 (top route) and line 7 (middle route) never touch at a station.
- Line 1 and line 3 are both horizontal and never touch.

That makes 3 groups, so 3 colours are enough. And 3 are needed because line 1, line 2 and line 4 all share stations with each other.

**Answer: (A) 3**

prompt: Dimitri wants to fold the shown net into a cube. If two areas share an edge, the triangles that are next to each other should have the same colour. How does he have to paint the triangles of the white square?

solutions.title: Match each edge of the white square
solutions.body:
The white square becomes the back face. Each of its four edges meets another face:

- **Left edge** meets the square right next to it: both triangles there are dark, so the white square's left triangles are dark.
- **Right edge** folds around to meet the left edge of the far-left square: there the upper triangle is light and the lower one dark.
- **Top edge** meets the top edge of the top square, but reversed (left↔right): so the top-left triangle is light and the top-right dark.
- **Bottom edge** meets the bottom edge of the bottom square, also reversed: bottom-left dark, bottom-right light.

Only (B) has all eight triangles like this.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Rule out with the easiest edges
solutions.body:
- The left edge of the white square touches the square to its left, with no folding tricks. That square's two triangles along that edge are dark. So the white square's two left-edge triangles must be dark. This rules out pictures where a left-edge triangle is light.
- The right edge wraps around to the far-left square, whose left edge has light on top and dark below. This rules out pictures with a different right edge.

Among the pictures, only (B) passes both tests (and its top and bottom also fit).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Mary wants to write the numbers 1 to 8 in the corners of the cube. For each of the six sides, the sum of the four numbers at the corners should be the same. She has already entered the numbers 6, 7 and 8 (see picture). What number does Mary have to write in the corner with the question mark?

solutions.title: Find the face sum first
solutions.body:
The top face and bottom face together use all 8 corners once: $1 + 2 + \dots + 8 = 36$. So each face sums to $36 \div 2 = 18$.

- **Right face** has 8, 7 and two empty corners (front top and back bottom). These two must add to $18 - 15 = 3$, so they are 1 and 2.
- **Bottom face** has ?, 8, 6 and the back-bottom-right corner (one of 1, 2). So ? + that corner $= 18 - 14 = 4$.
- If that corner were 2, then ? would be 2 as well — not allowed. So it is 1, and $? = 3$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Check the full cube
solutions.body:
Face sum is 18 (opposite faces together use all numbers $1$ to $8$, total 36).

With ? = 3, back-bottom-right = 1, front-top-right = 2, the remaining numbers 4 and 5 go on the front-top-left and back-top-left corners. Left face: $3 + 6 + 4 + 5 = 18$. Bottom: $3 + 8 + 1 + 6 = 18$. Right: $8 + 1 + 7 + 2 = 18$. Choosing 5 at front-top-left and 4 at back-top-left, front: $3 + 8 + 2 + 5 = 18$, back: $6 + 1 + 7 + 4 = 18$, top: $5 + 2 + 7 + 4 = 18$. Everything works!

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: Daniel wants to cut a rope into 12 equal pieces and marks the places where he has to cut. Mohammed wants to cut the same rope into 16 equal pieces and marks the cuts as well. Maya finally cuts the rope at all the marked spots. How many pieces does Maya get?

solutions.title: Count the cuts
solutions.body:
- 12 pieces need 11 cuts. 16 pieces need 15 cuts.
- Some marks are in the same place. Daniel's marks are at twelfths, Mohammed's at sixteenths. They match at $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ of the rope ($\frac{3}{12} = \frac{4}{16}$, and so on).
- Different cut places: $11 + 15 - 3 = 23$.

23 cuts make $23 + 1 = 24$ pieces.

**Answer: (A) 24**

solutions.title: Use a rope of length 48
solutions.body:
Imagine the rope is 48 cm long (48 is divisible by both 12 and 16).

- Daniel marks every 4 cm: 4, 8, ..., 44 (11 marks).
- Mohammed marks every 3 cm: 3, 6, ..., 45 (15 marks).
- Marks that are both: multiples of 12 → 12, 24, 36 (3 marks).

Different marks: $11 + 15 - 3 = 23$, so $24$ pieces.

**Answer: (A) 24**

prompt: The following image shows a honeycomb with 16 cells. Some cells (but not all) are filled with honey. The numbers in the cells indicate how many of the neighbouring cells are filled with honey. How many cells of the honeycomb are filled with honey?

solutions.title: Start from the 0 and work along
solutions.body:
Think of the honeycomb as 7 columns (from left to right: 1 cell, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1 cells).

- The **0** on the far right: its neighbours, the 3 and the 2 in column 6, are empty.
- The 3 in column 6 (upper) has 4 neighbours, and one of them (the 2 below it) is empty. So the other three are full: the 0, and the top 2 and the middle 3 of column 5.
- The 2 in column 6 (lower) already sees two full cells (the 0 and the middle 3 of column 5), so the lower 3 of column 5 is empty.
- That lower 3 of column 5 has 4 neighbours, one of them empty (the 2 in column 6), so the other three are full: the middle 3 of column 5, the lower 4 of column 4, and the bottom 1 of column 4.
- The bottom 1 of column 4 already sees the lower 4, so the lower 4 of column 3 is empty. That 4 has exactly 4 neighbours, so all of them are full: the lower 2 of column 2, the middle 3 of column 3, the lower 4 of column 4 and the bottom 1.
- The left 1 already sees the full lower 2 of column 2, so the upper 3 of column 2 is empty.
- The lower 2 of column 2 sees the full middle 3 of column 3, while the upper 3 of column 2 and the 4 of column 3 are empty. Its second full neighbour must be the left 1.
- Finally the middle 3 of column 5 needs one more full neighbour: the upper 4 of column 4.

Full cells: left 1, lower 2 of column 2, middle 3 of column 3, both 4s in the middle of column 4, bottom 1, top 2 and middle 3 of column 5, and the 0. That is **9** cells.

**Answer: (C) 9**

solutions.title: Check the solution
solutions.body:
Mark these 9 cells as full: the 1 on the left, the lower 2 of the second column, the middle 3 of the third column, the two 4s in the centre column, the 1 at the bottom, the top 2 and middle 3 of the fifth column, and the 0 on the right.

Now check some numbers:

- The 0 has no full neighbours ✓
- The left 1 has one full neighbour (the 2 next to it) ✓
- The top 2 of the centre column touches the upper 4 and the top 2 of column 5 ✓
- The lower 4 of the third column touches the lower 2, the middle 3, the lower 4 and the bottom 1 ✓

All 16 numbers fit, and each step of the other approach was forced, so the answer is unique: **9** cells.

**Answer: (C) 9**

prompt: There are three identical dice on a table. What is the sum of the three numbers that are on the bottom of the dice and touching the table?

solutions.title: Start with 22
solutions.body:
The six numbers on each die are 5, 8, 13, 17, 22 and 34. Two numbers seen together on one die can't be opposite.

- 22 is seen with 34 and 8 (die 1) and with 17 and 13 (die 3). So **22 is opposite 5**.
- Left are 8, 13, 17, 34. The 8 is seen with 34 (die 1) and with 13 (die 2), so **8 is opposite 17**.
- The last pair: **13 is opposite 34**.

Bottoms: die 1 (34 on top) → 13; die 2 (5 on top) → 22; die 3 (17 on top) → 8.

Sum: $13 + 22 + 8 = 43$.

**Answer: (C) 43**

solutions.title: Use the numbers seen on two dice
solutions.body:
Numbers seen together on one die are neighbours, so they are not opposite each other.

- 13 is on die 2 (with 5 and 8) and on die 3 (with 17 and 22). Its four neighbours are 5, 8, 17, 22, so the opposite of 13 is **34**.
- 8 is on die 1 (with 34 and 22) and on die 2 (with 5 and 13). Its opposite is the only number left: **17**.
- So 5 and 22 are opposite.

The top faces are 34, 5 and 17, so the bottoms are 13, 22 and 8: $13 + 22 + 8 = 43$.

**Answer: (C) 43**
